data:
This course is about the most intractable genre of political
 conflict. This type of conflict arises when two or more contending entities—which
 may be nation-states, and/or communities that self-define as ‘nations’—assert
 ownership (sovereignty) over the same territory. The competing claims to ownership
 of/sovereignty over the same land have often given rise to bitter, protracted conflicts,
 viewed through a zero-sum lens by the antagonists. What is common to the
 polarized antagonists is that all invoke the right to national self-determination (NSD)
 in support of their claim. The conflicts produced by these clashing aspirations to NSD
 are highly resistant to accommodation and compromise. The violent enmities they
 often generate further entrenches polarization and condemn entire world regions to
 prolonged instability. NSD conflicts are a global phenomenon—examples are found all over the world in
 recent and current times. Structured in a comparative case-study format, this course
 looks in depth at five such conflicts in the contemporary Middle East (the case of
 Israel and the Palestinians), South Asia or the Indian subcontinent (the cases of
 Kashmir and Sri Lanka), the Balkans region or southeastern Europe (the post-
 Yugoslav case of Bosnia-Hercegovina), and western Europe (the case of Northern
 Ireland). Students are exposed to the specific histories and contexts of these cases
 but are also encouraged to think and analyze comparatively across countries and
 world regions. The course is particularly focused on the great challenges of buildingpeace processes and crafting peace settlements in NSD conflicts. The course will be
 offered in the second trimester of the 2025-26 academic year.
